{{short description|American physicist (1932–1979)}}
'''Jon Mathews''' (1932–1979) was a physicist, yachtsman, scholar, and adventurer. After a 23-year career as a physics professor, he was lost at sea and presumed drowned during a circumnavigation attempt with his wife Jean in 1979.<ref>{{Cite web| title=Jon Mathews 1932-1979 | url=http://calteches.library.caltech.edu/582/2/Mathews.pdf | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100717135014/http://calteches.library.caltech.edu/582/2/Mathews.pdf | archive-date=2010-07-17}}</ref>

==Early life and education==
Mathews was born in [[Los Angeles, California]], the son of John H. “Jack” Mathews, an attorney, and Grace Logie Mathews, a schoolteacher. His paternal grandfather was Los Angeles city attorney [[W.B. Mathews]]. He grew up in Hollywood, graduated from the Flintridge Preparatory School, and enrolled in [[Pomona College]] in 1948 at the age of 16. As a sophomore, he met Charlotte Dallett, a chemistry student. Mathews also played shortstop for two years on Pomona’s baseball team. In June 1952, Mathews and Charlotte were married. He then graduated [[Latin honors|summa cum laude]] in Mathematics.

Mathews received a Fulbright Scholarship, and moved with Charlotte to England for his year of study at the [[University of Cambridge]]. In 1953, he continued his graduate studies at the [[California Institute of Technology]] in Pasadena, earning a PhD in 1956.<ref>[https://caltechcampuspubs.library.caltech.edu/2534/1/June_17,_1957.pdf "Sixty Third Annual Commencement Exercises"]. California Institute of Technology.</ref>

==Academic career==
After graduation, Mathews joined the Caltech staff.<ref>{{cite book|title=The Griffith Observer|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=izpBAQAAIAAJ|year=1954|publisher=Griffith Observatory|page=70}}</ref> In 1959 he was an assistant professor of physics,<ref>{{cite book|title=Directory of Academic Physicists|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=54FYAAAAMAAJ|year=1959|publisher=American Association of Physics Teachers}}</ref> in 1966 an Associate Professor<ref>{{cite book|title=ESI Quarterly Report|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Dm9LAAAAYAAJ|year=1966|publisher=Educational Services Incorporated.}}</ref> and in 1970 he held the position of full professor.<ref name="Foundation1970">{{cite book|author=Woodrow Wilson National Fellowship Foundation|title=Report for ...|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=OKE8AAAAIAAJ|year=1970|publisher=The Foundation}}</ref>

In 1964, Mathews moved his family of six from [[Altadena, California]], to Kanpur, India for a year while he participated in the Kanpur Indo-American Program (KIAP).<ref>{{Cite web| title=Report from Kanpur | url=http://calteches.library.caltech.edu/663/2/Kanpur.pdf | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100806002519/http://calteches.library.caltech.edu/663/2/Kanpur.pdf | archive-date=2010-08-06}}</ref>

In 1964, Mathews and his Caltech contemporary, Dr. Robert Walker, co-authored and published ''Mathematical Methods of Physics'',<ref>{{cite book|title=Quarterly of Applied Mathematics|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=fwErAQAAMAAJ|year=1965|publisher=G. Banta}}</ref> which received positive reviews<ref>{{cite book|title=Engineering and Science|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=QTRIAQAAIAAJ|year=1963|publisher=California Institute of Technology.}}</ref><ref>[https://www.science.org/doi/abs/10.1126/science.146.3642.388 Mathematical Methods of Physics. Jon Mathews and R. L. Walker. Benjamin, New York, 1964. xii + 475 pp. Illus. $12.50<!-- Bot generated title -->]</ref><ref name="Trefil2013">{{cite book|author=J. S. Trefil|title=Introduction to the Physics of Fluids and Solids|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=G7I3BQAAQBAJ&pg=PA275|date=November 6, 2013|publisher=Elsevier Science|isbn=978-1-4831-8739-6|pages=275–}}</ref> and remains a widely used college textbook in 2014.<ref name="Taylor2005">{{cite book|author=John Robert Taylor|title=Classical Mechanics|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=P1kCtNr-pJsC&pg=PA748|year=2005|publisher=University Science Books|isbn=978-1-891389-22-1|pages=748–}}</ref>

During his years at [[Caltech]], Mathews authored a number of scientific papers.<ref name="Kennefick2007">{{cite book|author=Daniel Kennefick|title=Traveling at the Speed of Thought: Einstein and the Quest for Gravitational Waves|url=https://archive.org/details/travelingatspeed0000kenn|url-access=registration|year=2007|publisher=Princeton University Press|isbn=978-0-691-11727-0|pages=[https://archive.org/details/travelingatspeed0000kenn/page/309 309]–}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|title=Nuclear Science Abstracts|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=OuCGF3zT7-gC|year=1970|publisher=Oak Ridge Directed Operations, Technical Information Division|page=3979}}</ref>

[[Deepak Dhar]] was his Ph.D. student.

==Search and Rescue==
Mathews also served on the Sierra Madre Search & Rescue Team from 1955 to 1962,<ref name=autogenerated3>[http://www.afamilyofthewest.org/9lalacey/07smsar.htm "Salute To Search And Rescue Team"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110212121537/http://www.afamilyofthewest.org/9lalacey/07smsar.htm |date=2011-02-12 }}. ''Sierra Madre News''.</ref><ref>[https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=1955&dat=19580213&id=ZHotAAAAIBAJ&sjid=cZgFAAAAIBAJ&pg=3982,5258884 "Youth Dies on Ledge"]. ''Reading Eagle''.</ref><ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/newspage/51723937/ "They Climb Mountains to Save Lives"]. ''The Times'' from San Mateo, California · April 11, 1964 Page 57</ref> using his climbing skills to rescue hikers and climbers in distress.<ref>Coutant, Martha Wood. [https://www.newspapers.com/image/19216133/ "Lifeguards of the Sierra Madre"]. ''Independent Press-Telegram'' from Long Beach, California ·November 26, 1961 Page 84</ref>

==Personal life==
The marriage of Mathews and Charlotte lasted 22 years and produced four children. The pair separated in 1974 and divorced in 1977. Mathews married his second wife, Jean Box Vontobel, in October 1977.

Mathews participated in sailing, hiking, tennis, chess, music, and travel. He played piano and clarinet, and learned several languages, including Mandarin Chinese.

In June 1979, Mathews and his wife Jean left Marina del Rey, California, aboard their 34-foot yacht Drambuie II to begin a planned 12-month circumnavigation attempt. The Drambuie made port in Hawaii, Palmyra Island, American Samoa, and several ports in Australia. The pair departed Perth, Australia in November 1979, heading westward towards Durban, South Africa. On December 23, 1979, the Drambuie sailed into the path of Cyclone Claudette,<ref name=autogenerated2>[https://www.australiasevereweather.com/tropical_cyclones/1979_1980/jtwc/tropical_cyclone_viola-claudette.htm Tropical Cyclone Tracks Maps : VIOLA-CLAUDETTE – Southern Hemisphere Season 1979 – 1980 Hurricanes Typhoons Joint Typhoon Warning Centre JTWC Data<!-- Bot generated title -->]</ref> a major storm with recorded wind gusts of over 150 knots. Radio contact was lost the next day.<ref>[http://jplarc.ampr.org/calling/1980/feb/feb80.html "N6BMY Lost at Sea, by Pete Mason, N6BBP"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20041107041849/http://jplarc.ampr.org/calling/1980/feb/feb80.html |date=2004-11-07 }}. ''W6VIO Calling'', JPL Amateur Radio Club newsletter, February 1980.</ref> No trace of the Drambuie or its occupants was ever found.<ref>Walden, Patrick. [https://web.archive.org/web/20160304222922/https://www.triumf.info/wiki/pwalden/index.php/Outliers;_A_book_review "Outliers; A book review"]. ''TRIUMF''.</ref>
